```{=html}
<div class="publication" id="pub-takeup">
<p>Education providers’ take-up of government grants: Evidence from a grant allocation discontinuity (with Olof Rosenqvist)</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-takeup"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-takeup"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-takeup"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-takeup"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>In decentralized school systems where core funding comes from local governments, education providers can sometimes be entitled to central government grants on top of the core funding (e.g. Title I in the US). In Sweden, government grants that public and private education providers can claim have grown over time; from around 3 % of compulsory school costs in 2010 to 7 % in 2023. The grants, which typically are tied to specific purposes, are a way for the government to exercise control over various school policies in a decentralized system. However, for the grants to have an impact, the providers must claim their entitlements which requires submitting a detailed plan for fund usage and not all providers do this, especially not smaller private providers. We study how the size of the grant entitlement affects providers’ take-up decisions. This is a margin that readily can be adjusted by e.g. merging smaller grants to a single larger. We exploit variation from a large grant in Sweden that allocated substantially more money to providers with a socioeconomic student composition below a certain threshold value. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that take-up among private providers increased from 70 % to 88 % as the grant amount increased from about 4 % to 13 % of the total cost per student. Importantly, the effect on take-up appears to be sticky as it remains in a later year when the compensatory part was removed from the grant and all providers were entitled to the same amount per student.</p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-equity">
<p>The effects of increasing compensatory resource allocation on student achievement: Evidence from the Equity grant in the Swedish compulsory school (with Olof Rosenqvist)</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-equity"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-equity"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-equity"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-equity"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Substantial and persistent differences in learning outcomes between schools largely caused by school segregation is a recurrent issue in many countries and is seen as a threat against equality of opportunity. Compensatory resource allocation policies are sometimes used to mitigate this problem, but the evidence on the effects of such policies is limited. In this paper, we evaluate a large compensatory grant in Sweden, the Equity grant, which was launched by the government in 2017/2018 with the aim of improving the prospects of success for students with a disadvantaged background. The grant, which has since increased to more than SEK 7 billion per year, is allocated based on a socioeconomic index. We examine the relationship between education provider index and teacher-to-student ratio in the years before and after the introduction of the grant and find that teacher-to-student ratios are significantly more compensatory as the grant is introduced and then gradually expanded. Overall, however, we do not see that the increased teacher resources among providers serving disadvantaged students led to smaller test score differences between providers serving advantaged and disadvantaged students respectively. However, in grade 9, where the effect on class size is most pronounced, there are indications of improved student performance, which also translate into increased high-school enrollment.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-equity"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://ideas.repec.org/p/hhs/ifauwp/2025_015.html">[IFAU WP 2025:15]</a></p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-boards">
<p>Board quotas, women&#x27;s representation in top management, and firm performance (with Harini Annadanam and Aylin Shawkat)</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-boards"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-boards"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-boards"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-boards"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>This paper examines the effects of a gender quota on supervisory boards implemented in Germany in 2016, which mandated 106 large firms to have at least 30% of women on their supervisory boards. Applying a difference-in-differences approach to panel data on firms, we find that the introduction of the quota increased the share of firms complying with the quota law. We also find, however, that this positive effect originated from earlier attempts to introduce quotas for supervisory boards. We neither find that other characteristics of supervisory board members are affected, nor that the quota created spillover effects on the untargeted executive boards. For firm performance, we find, if any, positive effects of the quota introduction.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-boards"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="mailto:jan.sauermann@ifau.uu.se">[Most recent version – please email me]</a></p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-peer">
<p>Peer Effects in the Workplace: A Network Approach (with Matthew J. Lindquist and Yves Zenou)</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-peer"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-peer"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-peer"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-peer"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>We study both endogenous and exogenous peer effects in worker productivity using an explicit network approach. We apply this method to data from an in-house call center of a multinational mobile network operator that include detailed information on individual performance. We find that an increase in average co-worker current productivity increases worker productivity, while an increase in average co-worker permanent productivity decreases worker productivity. We also investigate when peer effects matter and show that the relative importance of these two types of peer effects depends on the volume of incoming calls.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-peer"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="mailto:jan.sauermann@ifau.uu.se">[Most recent version – please email me]</a> <a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/why-worker-productivity-contagious">[Voxeu.org]</a> <span class="pub-note">[Previously circulated as IZA DP No. 15131 and CEPR DP 10928]</span></p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-selection">
<p>Assessing Selection Bias in Non-experimental Estimates of the Returns to Workplace Training (with Anders Stenberg)</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-selection"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-selection"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-selection"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-selection"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>We assess selection bias in estimated returns to workplace training by exploiting a field experiment in which workers were randomly assigned to a one-week training program. Using the causal estimate of the effect of the training program on worker productivity as a benchmark, we compare it to non-experimental estimates that is estimated using a sample who were chosen not to participate in the field experiment. Because the latter group is (potentially) endogenously selected, we expect the non-experimental estimates to be biased due to unobservable characteristics. The results show that non-experimental estimates are biased, yielding estimated returns of up to twice as high as the causal returns. We show that when controlling for pre-treatment performance, individual fixed effects, as well as applying entropy matching, only a very small bias remains.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-selection"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="mailto:jan.sauermann@ifau.uu.se">[Most recent version – please email me]</a> <span class="pub-note">[Previously released as IZA DP 13789]</span></p></div></details>
```

## Peer-reviewed publications

```{=html}
<div class="publication" id="pub-ClemensSauermann2025">
<p>Clemens, Marco, and Jan Sauermann (2025), <em>Making the right call: The heterogeneous effects of individual performance pay on productivity</em>, <strong><em>Labour Economics</em></strong>, 94 (June), 102694</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-ClemensSauermann2025"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-ClemensSauermann2025"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-ClemensSauermann2025"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-ClemensSauermann2025"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Performance pay has been shown to have important implications for worker and firm productivity. Although workers’ skills may directly matter for the cost of effort to reach performance goals, surprisingly little is know about the heterogeneity in the effects of incentive pay across workers. In this study, we apply a dynamic difference-in-differences estimator to the introduction of a generous bonus pay program to study how salient performance thresholds affect incentivized and non-incentivized performance outcomes for low- and high-skilled workers. While we do find that individual incentive pay did not affect workers’ performance on average, we show that this result conceals an underlying heterogeneity in the response to individual performance pay: individual performance pay has a significant effect on the performance of high-skilled workers but not for low-skilled workers. The findings can be rationalized with the idea that the costs of effort differ by workers’ skill level. We also explore whether agents alter their overtime hours and find a negative effect, possibly avoiding negative consequences of longer working hours.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-ClemensSauermann2025"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/labeco/v94y2025ics0927537125000211.html">[publisher version (open access)]</a> <span class="pub-note">[previously released as IZA DP17119 and IFAU WP 2025:6]</span></p>

<div class="publication" id="pub-Adermonetal2024">
<p>Adermon, Adrian, Lisa Laun, Patrik Lind, Martin Olsson, Jan Sauermann, and Anna Sjögren (2024), <em>Earnings Losses and the Role of the Welfare State during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evidence from Sweden</em>, <strong><em>Review of Income and Wealth</em></strong>, 70(4), pp. 981–1010</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-Adermonetal2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-Adermonetal2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-Adermonetal2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-Adermonetal2024"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Many governments introduced temporary adjustments to counter the economic and health consequences of the COVID‐19 pandemic. We study the importance of already‐existing government transfers and new pandemic measures to mitigate individual income losses during the onset of the pandemic in Sweden using a difference‐in‐differences approach and population‐wide data on monthly earnings and government transfer payments. We find that labor earnings dropped by 2.7 percent in 2020. Existing transfers and new pandemic measures reduced earnings losses to 1.5 percent. These average effects mask considerable differences in earnings losses, which were, by and large, evened out by existing transfers and new pandemic measures.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-Adermonetal2024"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/revinw/v70y2024i4p981-1010.html">[publisher version (open access)]</a> <span class="pub-note">[previously released as IZA DP15662, IFAU WP 2022:20 and IFN WP 1443]</span> <span class="pub-note">[financed by Vetenskapsrådet]</span></p>
<p><scopus-citations file="citations/AdermonLaunLindOlssonSauermannSjogren2024_raw.txt"></scopus-citations></p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-ButschekSauermann2024">
<p>Butschek, Sebastian, and Jan Sauermann (2024), <em>The Effect of Employment Protection on Firms&#x27; Worker Selection</em>, <strong><em>Journal of Human Resources</em></strong>, 59(6), pp. 1981–2020</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-ButschekSauermann2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-ButschekSauermann2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-ButschekSauermann2024"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-ButschekSauermann2024"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>To estimate the causal effect of employment protection on firms’ worker selection, we study a policy change that reduced dismissal costs for the employers of more than a tenth of Sweden’s workforce. Our difference‐in‐differences analysis of firms’ hiring uses individual ability measures, including estimated worker fixed effects, GPA at age 15, and military test scores. We find that the reform reduced minimum hire quality by around 2 percent. Our results show that firms both decreased their hiring thresholds and hired more workers. We find that firms increasingly hired young, foreign‐born, and long‐term nonemployed individuals, suggesting potential welfare gains from the reform.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-ButschekSauermann2024"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://jhr.uwpress.org/content/early/2022/05/02/jhr.0919-10433R1.abstract">[publisher version (gated)]</a> <a href="files/ButschekSauermann_EPL.pdf">[preprint]</a> <a href="files/ButschekSauermann_EPL_onlineappendix.pdf">[online appendix]</a> <span class="pub-note">[previously released as IZA DP 12305]</span> <span class="pub-note">[financed by Jan Wallanders och Tom Hedelius stiftelse samt Tore Browaldhs stiftelse]</span></p>
<p><scopus-citations file="citations/ButschekSauermann2024_raw.txt"></scopus-citations></p></div></details>

We find that the reform reduced minimum hire quality by around 2 percent. Our results show that firms both decreased their hiring thresholds and hired more workers. We find that firms increasingly hired young, foreign‐born, and long‐term nonemployed individuals, suggesting potential welfare gains from the reform.},
  number = {6},
  pages = {1981--2020},
  url = {https://jhr.uwpress.org/content/early/2022/05/02/jhr.0919-10433R1.abstract}
}</code></pre></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-EngbomMoserSauermann2023">
<p>Engbom, Niklas, Christian Moser, and Jan Sauermann (2023), <em>Firm Pay Dynamics</em>, <strong><em>Journal of Econometrics</em></strong>, 233(3), pp. 396–423</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-EngbomMoserSauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-EngbomMoserSauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-EngbomMoserSauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-EngbomMoserSauermann2023"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>We study the nature of firm pay dynamics. To this end, we propose a statistical model that extends the seminal framework by Abowd et al. (1999) to allow for idiosyncratically time-varying firm pay policies. We estimate the model using linked employer–employee data for Sweden from 1985 to 2016. By drawing on detailed firm financials data, we show that firms that become more productive and accumulate capital raise pay, whereas firms lower pay as they add workers. A secular increase in firm-year pay dispersion in Sweden since 1985 is accounted for by greater persistence of firm pay among incumbent firms as well as greater dispersion in firm pay among entrant firms, as opposed to more volatile firm pay.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-EngbomMoserSauermann2023"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304407622000653">[publisher version (open access)]</a> <span class="pub-note">[previously released as CEPR DP 16922, IZA DP 15014, NBER WP 29697]</span></p>

<div class="publication" id="pub-Sauermann2023">
<p>Sauermann, Jan (2023), <em>Worker Reciprocity and the Returns to Training: Evidence from a Field Experiment</em>, <strong><em>Journal of Economics &amp; Management Strategy</em></strong>, 32(3), pp. 543–557</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-Sauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-Sauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-Sauermann2023"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-Sauermann2023"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Do reciprocal workers have higher returns to employer-sponsored training? Using a field experiment with random assignment to training combined with survey information on workers&#x27; reciprocal inclinations, the results show that reciprocal workers reciprocate employers&#x27; training investments by higher posttraining performance. This result, which is robust to controlling for observed personality traits and worker fixed effects, suggests that individuals reciprocate the firm&#x27;s human capital investment with higher effort, in line with theoretical models on gift exchange in the workplace. This finding provides an alternative rationale to explain firm training investments even with the risk of poaching.</p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019">
<p>Mengel, Friederike, Jan Sauermann, and Ulf Zölitz (2019), <em>Gender Bias in Teaching Evaluations</em>, <strong><em>Journal of the European Economic Association</em></strong>, 17(2), pp. 535-566</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>This paper provides new evidence on gender bias in teaching evaluations. We exploit a quasi-experimental dataset of 19,952 student evaluations of university faculty in a context where students are randomly allocated to female or male instructors. Despite the fact that neither students’ grades nor self-study hours are affected by the instructor’s gender, we find that women receive systematically lower teaching evaluations than their male colleagues. This bias is driven by male students’ evaluations, is larger for mathematical courses, and particularly pronounced for junior women. The gender bias in teaching evaluations we document may have direct as well as indirect effects on the career progression of women by affecting junior women’s confidence and through the reallocation of instructor resources away from research and toward teaching.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-MengelSauermannZoelitz2019"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://academic.oup.com/jeea/article-abstract/17/2/535/4850534">[publisher version (open access)]</a> <a href="files/MengelSauermannZoelitz_GenderBias_OnlineApp.pdf">[online appendix]</a></p>

<div class="publication" id="pub-DeGripFouargeSauermann2010">
<p>De Grip, Andries, Didier Fouarge, and Jan Sauermann (2010), <em>What Affects International Migration of Science and Engineering Graduates from Europe?</em>, <strong><em>Economics of Innovation and New Technology</em></strong>, 19(5), pp. 407–421</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-DeGripFouargeSauermann2010"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-DeGripFouargeSauermann2010"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-DeGripFouargeSauermann2010"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-DeGripFouargeSauermann2010"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Using a data set of science and engineering graduates from 12 European countries, we analyse the determinants of labour migration after graduation. We find that not only wage gains are driving the migration decision, but also differences in labour market opportunities, past migration experience and international student exchange are strong predictors of future migration. Contrary to our expectations, job characteristics such as the utilisation of skills in the job and involvement in innovation hardly affect the migration decision. When analysing country choice, countries such as the USA, Canada and Australia appear to attract migrants due to their larger R&amp;D intensity. Moreover, graduates with higher grades are more likely to migrate to these countries.</p></div></details>

<div class="publication" id="pub-ReinowskiSauermann2008">
<p>Reinowski, Eva, and Jan Sauermann (2008), <em>Does Temporary Employment Affect the Work-related Training of Low-skilled Employees?</em>, <strong><em>Journal for Labour Market Research</em></strong>, 41(4), pp. 489–499</p>
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-ReinowskiSauermann2008"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="moreinfo-ReinowskiSauermann2008"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show more information</button>
<button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="bibtex-ReinowskiSauermann2008"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show BibTeX</button></div>
<details id="abstract-ReinowskiSauermann2008"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Similar to other European countries, the use of fixed-term contracts in Germany has been deregulated since the 1980s. Though temporary employment can be seen as a possibility to re-enter the labour market, it is argued that temporary employment may lead to &#x27;dead-ends&#x27; and to lower investments in further training. From a theoretical perspective, there are arguments for higher and for lower investments in further training for employers and employees. Thus, it is not clear whether firms and employees invest differently when temporary contracts are used. Using the German Mikrozensus 2004, this paper analyses the effect of temporary contracts on work-related training for low-skilled workers. To take systematic differences between temporary and permanent employees into account, we estimate a bivariate probit model for whether fixed-term employment affects participation in work-related training. We conclude that holding a temporary contract does not have systematic disadvantages in access to further training. The use of temporary contracts does not therefore worsen the situation of low-skilled employees in terms of their human capital accumulation.</p></div></details>
<details id="moreinfo-ReinowskiSauermann2008"><summary hidden>Show more information</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p><a href="https://ideas.repec.org/a/iab/iabzaf/v41i4p489-499.html">[publisher version (open access)]</a></p></div></details>
```

```{=html}
<div class="pub-actions"><button class="pub-toggle" type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="abstract-Sauermann2023_WoL"><span class="tri" aria-hidden="true">▸</span> Show abstract</button>

<details id="abstract-Sauermann2023_WoL"><summary hidden>Show abstract</summary><div class="pub-detail"><p>Measuring workers’ productivity is important for public policy and private-sector decision-making. Due to the lack of a general measure that captures workers’ productivity, firms often use one- or multi-dimensional performance measures, which can be used, for example, to analyze how different incentive systems affect workers’ behavior. The public sector itself also uses measures to monitor and evaluate personnel, such as teachers. Policymakers and managers need to understand the advantages and disadvantages of the available metrics to select the right performance measures for their purpose.</p></div></details>
```

```{=html}
document.addEventListener('click', event => {
  const button = event.target.closest('.pub-toggle');
  if (!button) return;
  const target = document.getElementById(button.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
  const opening = !target.open;
  document.querySelectorAll('.publication details').forEach(panel => panel.open = false);
  document.querySelectorAll('.pub-toggle').forEach(control => {
    control.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
    control.querySelector('.tri').textContent = '▸';
  });
  target.open = opening;
  button.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(opening));
  button.querySelector('.tri').textContent = opening ? '▾' : '▸';
});
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
class ScopusCitations extends HTMLElement {
  async connectedCallback() {
    const file = this.getAttribute("file");
    const label = this.getAttribute("label") || "SCOPUS-citations";
    const prefix = this.getAttribute("prefix") ?? (label + ": ");
    const missing = this.getAttribute("missing") || ""; // what to show if fetch fails

    if (!file) {
      this.textContent = missing;
      return;
    }

    // Render a placeholder immediately
    this.textContent = prefix + "…";

    try {
      // Resolve relative paths correctly (works with/without baseurl, subfolders, etc.)
      const url = new URL(file, window.location.href).toString();

      const r = await fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" });
      if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`);

      const t = (await r.text()).trim();
      const m = t.match(/\d+/);          // raw file should be just digits, but be defensive
      if (!m) throw new Error("No number found");

      this.textContent = prefix + m[0];
    } catch (e) {
      // Fail quietly
      this.textContent = missing;
      // Uncomment for debugging:
      // console.warn("Scopus citation fetch failed:", file, e);
    }
  }
}

customElements.define("scopus-citations", ScopusCitations);
</script>
```
